title: The Passive Voice
summary: How the passive is formed in every tense, when to prefer it, and why intransitive verbs have no passive at all.

sections.heading: Form: be + past participle in every tense
sections.body:
The passive is built from the verb `be` in whatever tense is required, plus the past participle. Only `be` moves: `is done`, `is being done`, `was done`, `was being done`, `has been done`, `had been done`, `will be done`, `is going to be done`.

The participle never carries the tense, so the quickest repair is to check the auxiliary on its own. `The results are published last year` fails because `are` is in the wrong tense, not because of anything wrong with `published`.

examples.right: The findings are published in a peer-reviewed journal each spring.
examples.note: Present simple passive, for a regular and repeated event.

examples.right: The samples were being analysed when the power failed.
examples.wrong: The samples were analysing when the power failed.
examples.note: The continuous passive needs `being` in front of the participle.

examples.right: The bridge has been closed to traffic since Monday.
examples.wrong: The bridge is closed since Monday.
examples.note: `since` with an unfinished period calls for the present perfect passive.

examples.right: A new wing is going to be added to the hospital next year.
examples.note: `going to` is followed by the passive infinitive `be added`.

sections.heading: Passive infinitives, gerunds and modals
sections.body:
After another verb the passive appears in a non-finite form: the passive infinitive `to be done` and the passive gerund `being done`. The choice between them is decided by the word in front, exactly as it would be in the active. Compare `expect to be told` with `object to being told`, where that `to` is a preposition and therefore takes a gerund.

Modals take the bare passive infinitive: `must be submitted`, `can be arranged`, `should have been checked`. The modal itself never changes voice.

examples.right: All coursework must be submitted through the online portal.
examples.wrong: All coursework must submitted through the online portal.
examples.note: A modal is followed by `be` plus the participle, never by the participle alone.

examples.right: Several residents objected to being told about the plans so late.
examples.wrong: Several residents objected to be told about the plans so late.
examples.note: `object to` ends in a preposition, so the passive gerund is required.

examples.right: The equipment should have been calibrated before the first run.
examples.note: Perfect modal passive, typically used to criticise something left undone.

sections.heading: When the passive is the right choice
sections.body:
Three conditions favour the passive. The agent may be **unknown**, as in `The lock had been forced during the night`; it may be **irrelevant or obvious**, as in `The suspect was arrested on Tuesday`; or the writer may want the receiver of the action in **subject position**, which is where English puts the topic of the sentence.

Academic prose adds a fourth reason: the impersonal register. `The mixture was heated to 80°C` keeps the method in view and the experimenter out of it. This is a convention of style, not a rule of grammar, and an essay written wholly in the passive reads as heavy and evasive.

When an agent is worth mentioning it is introduced by `by`, and the instrument used is introduced by `with`. The two are not interchangeable: `The inscription was carved with a fine chisel by a local mason`.

examples.right: Two hundred questionnaires were distributed to first-year students.
examples.note: Who handed them out is irrelevant; the questionnaires are the topic.

examples.right: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.
examples.note: Here the agent is the point of the sentence, so the active is better.

examples.right: The report was written by an independent panel.
examples.wrong: The report was written from an independent panel.
examples.note: The agent is marked by `by`, never by `from`.

examples.right: The surface can be cleaned with a damp cloth.
examples.wrong: The surface can be cleaned by a damp cloth.
examples.note: A tool is an instrument, so it takes `with`.

sections.heading: The get-passive
sections.body:
In speech and informal writing `get` often replaces `be`: `got broken`, `got stolen`, `got promoted`. It suggests something sudden, unplanned, and usually to the subject's cost or benefit.

It remains a spoken form. In the writing tasks and in any academic register the expected version is `be`: write `The equipment was damaged in transit`, not `got damaged`. The distinction to learn is one of register rather than of correctness. The fixed expressions `get married`, `get dressed` and `get lost` behave the same way.

examples.right: Three laptops got stolen from the office during the refurbishment.
examples.note: Natural in speech: the event was sudden and unwelcome.

examples.right: Three laptops were stolen from the office during the refurbishment.
examples.note: The same fact in the register expected of a written answer.

examples.right: The proposal got rejected at the first meeting.
examples.wrong: The proposal got rejecting at the first meeting.
examples.note: `get` still requires the past participle.

sections.heading: Verbs with two objects
sections.body:
Verbs such as `give`, `send`, `offer`, `award`, `tell` and `pay` take two objects, so each has two possible passives. English strongly prefers the person as subject: `She was given a grant`. The alternative `A grant was given to her` is also correct but foregrounds the thing, and the preposition `to` then has to appear.

The frequent error is to promote the person and keep the preposition anyway, producing `She was given to a grant`.

examples.right: She was awarded a grant of £40,000 in her second year.
examples.wrong: She was awarded to a grant of £40,000 in her second year.
examples.note: With the person as subject, no preposition follows the verb.

examples.right: A grant of £40,000 was awarded to her in her second year.
examples.note: With the thing as subject, the person now needs `to`.

examples.right: The successful applicants were sent their contracts by email.
examples.note: The indirect object becomes the subject, which is the more natural version.

sections.heading: Intransitive verbs have no passive
sections.body:
A verb can be made passive only if it has an object to promote. `happen`, `occur`, `arrive`, `appear`, `disappear`, `rise`, `fall`, `die` and `belong` take no object, so they have no passive at all. `The accident was happened` is not merely unusual: it is ungrammatical, and it is one of the errors an examiner notices fastest.

The confusion is understandable, because the meaning feels passive — nobody chose for the accident to occur. English encodes that idea in the verb itself rather than in the voice.

examples.right: A serious accident happened on the coastal road.
examples.wrong: A serious accident was happened on the coastal road.
examples.note: `happen` is intransitive and cannot be passivised.

examples.right: The symptoms appeared three days after exposure.
examples.wrong: The symptoms were appeared three days after exposure.
examples.note: The same trap with `appear`, `occur` and `arrive`.

examples.right: The manuscript disappeared from the archive some time in the 1940s.
examples.wrong: The manuscript was disappeared from the archive.
examples.note: Compare the transitive `was removed`, which does have a passive.

slips: `was happened`, `was occurred`, `was arrived`: intransitive verbs have no passive. Write `happened`, `occurred`, `arrived`.
Dropping `being` from the continuous passive. `The road is repaired` describes a finished state; `is being repaired` means work is under way.
`carved by a fine chisel` for an instrument. Tools take `with`; only the doer takes `by`.
Keeping the preposition after a two-object passive: `She was given to a scholarship`. Drop `to` when the person is the subject.
A modal followed by a bare participle: `must submitted`. Modals need `be`: `must be submitted`.
`got damaged` in an academic answer. The get-passive is spoken register; in writing use `was damaged`.

questions.prompt: The bridge ___ twice since it opened, most recently after the floods of 2019.
questions.explain: `since it opened` measures a period running up to the present, which requires the present perfect passive. `was rebuilt` would need a finished time reference such as `in 2019`.

questions.prompt: Please excuse the noise: the roof ___ while the museum remains open to visitors.
questions.explain: Work in progress at the moment of speaking takes `is being` plus the past participle; `is repaired` would describe a finished state instead.

questions.prompt: All applications ___ through the online portal by 5 p.m. on Friday.
questions.explain: A modal is followed by the bare passive infinitive `be submitted`. `must submit` is active and would make the applications the ones doing the submitting.

questions.prompt: Several residents objected to ___ about the plans so late in the process.
questions.explain: The `to` of `object to` is a preposition, so it takes the passive gerund. `to be told` would follow a verb such as `expect`, where `to` belongs to the infinitive.

questions.prompt: The revised guidelines ___ next month, according to the ministry's website.
questions.explain: `will` takes the bare passive infinitive `be published`; a participle on its own cannot carry future reference.

questions.prompt: A serious accident ___ on the coastal road early yesterday morning.
questions.explain: `happen` takes no object, so it has no passive form; the same holds for `occur`, and `take place` is likewise used only in the active.

questions.prompt: Two of the laptops ___ from the staff room while the building was being refurbished.
questions.explain: The get-passive suits a sudden and unwelcome event in speech; in a written answer the expected register would be `were stolen`.

questions.prompt: The successful applicants ___ their contracts by email last Friday.
questions.explain: `send` takes two objects, and English prefers the person as passive subject with no preposition after the verb. `were sent to` would leave `their contracts` stranded, and `was sent` does not agree with the plural subject.

questions.prompt: The note had been written ___ a fountain pen, in careful capital letters.
questions.explain: A pen is an instrument rather than an agent, so it takes `with` or `using`; `by` is reserved for the person who performed the action.

questions.prompt: The council has confirmed that the old market ___ into flats; work starts in June.
questions.explain: `going to` is followed by the passive infinitive `be converted`. `is going to convert` would make the market itself the agent of the conversion.

questions.prompt: Nobody knows exactly when the manuscript ___ from the cathedral archive.
questions.explain: `disappear` is intransitive, so `was disappeared` is impossible; the active past simple already conveys that nobody deliberately caused it.

questions.prompt: The theory was first proposed ___ a young German physicist in 1905.
questions.explain: The agent of a passive is introduced by `by`. `from` marks a source and `with` an instrument, and neither fits a person who performed the action.
